newsitem.title: GERMANY: Hundreds of angry German builders storm Reichstag.
newsitem.headline: Hundreds of angry German builders storm Reichstag.

text.p: Hundreds of German construction workers broke through barricades and stormed the building site at Berlin's Reichstag on Friday as they gathered to cap five days of protests over chronic unemployment in their industry.

Police guarding the building that will become Germany's parliament again in 1999 stood by helplessly as the angry workers threw stones and bottles at the prefabricated huts for building crews, made up mostly of cheap foreign labour.

Some protestors also grappled with police and smashed a window after storming the nearby Hotel Adlon, a luxury landmark destroyed in World War Two and now being rebuilt. Police have found several illegal workers there in the past.
About 6,000 builders then marched from the Brandenburg Gate to the city centre to demonstrate against job losses in their stricken sector and so-called "wage-dumping" by foreign firms.
"Sometime the bomb will explode. My God, we don't want to be violent but sometimes it comes down to that," one builder said.
Unions say 400,000 German building workers are unemployed.

The protests capped a week of marches and vigils on the Potsdamer Platz, Europe's largest building site. Earlier negotiators, trying to reach a wage agreement in the sector, said they had failled to strike a deal on Thursday. They agreed to meet on March 25 to make a fresh attempt.
Dieter Schulte, head of the German Trade Union Federation (DGB), blamed the government for supporting "modern-day slavery" by allowing foreign workers to undercut wages.
"With unrestricted deregulation, the government is promoting competition from workers from the whole of Europe," Schulte told builders at the rally.
Building union officials expressed solidarity with coal miners who beseiged Bonn this week and won some concessions from the government on Thursday over planned subsidy cuts.

"It (the miners' protest) shows that resistance is worth it. But it also shows that the problems we have, the miners, but in particular the builders, are not taken seriously by the public," Rainer Knerler, Berlin head of the IB Bau construction workers' union, told German radio.
"Who has heard about our protest action of almost half a million unemployed builders? Everyone who comes through Berlin sees all the building sites and thinks the boom is unbroken," Knerler said.
Schulte said tens of thousands of builders were out of work in Berlin despite a massive building programme that has turned the centre of the city into a confusing obstacle course.
Most of the work goes to foreigners from as far afield as Portugal, Britain, Ireland, Poland and Russia.
IG Bau is seeking new clauses compensating workers for pay lost as a result of bad weather and wants a "13th month" bonus cancelled from existing contracts to be reinstated.
The union also wants to stop foreigners illegally working on construction sites and undercutting wages.
IG Bau has not yet stated its wage demands but wants to keep wages from falling in real terms. It says there are 1.3 million working in the sector and 400,000 more out of a job.

In Bonn, parliament held a heated debate about Germany's record 4.7 million unemployment and the government defended a 25 billion mark ($14.7 billion) investment package Chancellor Helmut Kohl announced on Wednesday in a drive to create jobs.
Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt saw chances of fighting against unemployment. "Orders are rising and investment is beginning to pick up," he told parliament.

But economists said Kohl's investment package would not change their growth forecasts for 1997 and make no real dent in Germany's record post-war unemployment. They considered it largely a political measure. ($ = 1.705 German Marks)
